item.title: XMLHttpRequest: six years waiting for a name
item.description: Microsoft shipped the object behind every web application in 1999, under a name its author calls an excuse. Almost nobody used it until a designer's 2005 essay called the technique Ajax.
item.content:encoded:
The most important line of JavaScript of the 2000s shipped in 1999 with a name its own author calls an excuse, and then sat largely ignored for six years until somebody gave the technique around it a better one.

var req = new ActiveXObject(
  "Microsoft.XMLHTTP");

That is how you asked a server for something without leaving the page, in Internet Explorer 5, in March 1999. It isn't JavaScript's doing, strictly. ActiveXObject was Microsoft's way of letting script load a Windows component, the same door that opened Excel or the file system, and "Microsoft.XMLHTTP" was a component that happened to speak HTTP. The object it handed back could open a URL, send a request and give you the response as text. The page stayed where it was.

Every web application you use now is built on that ability. What I find worth an essay is the gap. The capability was in the dominant browser from 1999. The word "Ajax" arrived on February 18, 2005. In between, the object sat in the most widely used browser on earth and drew very little notice. The story of those six years is a story about a team with a deadline, a browser plug-in system, a recession and, in the end, a consultant who needed a shorter word for a client meeting.

Before: one click, one page

The web's original contract was simple. You clicked, the browser threw away the page, the server built a new one, and you waited. Jesse James Garrett, in the essay this story ends with, put the cost in one line: "While the server is doing its thing, what's the user doing? That's right, waiting."

Dynamic HTML, which arrived in 1997 and which split the web in two for a while, let a page change itself after it loaded. It did not let a page fetch anything new. Script could rearrange what the server had already sent, and that was all. If you wanted to check whether a username was taken, you submitted the form.

People found ways around this, and they were all smuggling operations. Anything with a src could carry a message to the server, so the standard trick was a frame the visitor couldn't see:

<iframe name="rpc" width="0" height="0"></iframe>

<script>
function checkName(name) {
  frames["rpc"].location =
    "check.asp?name=" + escape(name);
}
function gotResult(taken) {
  alert(taken ? "Taken" : "Available");
}
</script>

The server answered with a tiny HTML page whose only content was a script calling parent.gotResult(true). The response was, in effect, a function call sent as a web page. That is the Internet Explorer form; other browsers needed other hidden elements for the same trick. It failed in ways that were hard to see, because a hidden frame has no error handler and no status code you can read.

Microsoft had an official product in this space too. Brent Ashley's Remote Scripting page, which Ashley has kept online "for historical purposes", describes Microsoft Remote Scripting as solving the problem "by embedding a Java applet in the page to communicate with the server". A Java applet, to send a string. Ashley wrote a JavaScript-only alternative called JSRS "in the summer of 2000", built on hidden DHTML elements, and a second one called RSLite that passed its data in cookies. When people are carrying data in cookies on purpose, the platform is missing a feature.

A weekend in Redmond

The feature came from a mail team. Alex Hopmann, who worked on Exchange 2000 at Microsoft, wrote the history down in The Story of XMLHTTP, and it is the best primary source on any of this, so I'll lean on it.

Exchange needed a new Outlook Web Access, the webmail front end for corporate email. Hopmann dates the start to "probably sometime in late 1998". Two versions got underway: one of plain HTML pages, and one built with DHTML by Jim Van Eaton and Bob Gering. Of the first demo of the DHTML one, Hopmann writes, "I was just blown away". The DHTML one had a plumbing problem, though. In Hopmann's words, "they were basically doing hacky form-posts back to the server". So:

That weekend I startup up Visual Studio and whipped up the first version of what would become XMLHTTP. The first version didn't have async support hooked up and was pretty crude…

A component on one developer's machine doesn't help a product whose whole pitch is that you can walk up to any computer and read your mail. It had to be in the browser already. Internet Explorer 5 was, by Hopmann's account, "just weeks away from beta 2", its last beta. Another developer, Shawn Bracewell, rewrote the code to production quality and added the asynchronous mode and error handling. Hopmann, meanwhile, went looking for something that already shipped with Internet Explorer and could carry a stowaway. That turned out to be MSXML, Microsoft's XML parser library, whose team was run by Jean Paoli.

Which brings us to the name. I'd assumed for years that it was called XMLHTTP because it was designed to fetch XML. Hopmann says otherwise:

…the thing is mostly about HTTP and doesn't have any specific tie to XML other than that was the easiest excuse for shipping it so I needed to cram XML into the name (plus- XML was the hot technology at the time and it seemed like some good marketing for the component).

Two other lines from that account deserve to be better known. On security: "We did a quick security review but at the time no one really understood the seriousness or types of vulnerabilities that anything shipping could cause." And on quality: "no one other than OWA is going to try to call it so if it has a bug in the beta, worst case we just can't use it." The feature that would carry Gmail, Google Suggest and much of what got called Web 2.0 was checked in a week before a beta, on the theory that only one team would ever call it.

Internet Explorer 5 shipped in March 1999. Exchange 2000 and its Outlook Web Access followed, per Hopmann, "another year and a half" later. By then the piece it needed was on a great many desktops.

How the object worked

The API that went out in 1999 is, with small changes, the one in your browser today. A full request, as you'd have written it for Internet Explorer 5 or 6:

var req = new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
req.onreadystatechange = function () {
  if (req.readyState == 4) {
    if (req.status == 200) {
      document.all["news"].innerHTML =
        req.responseText;
    }
  }
};
req.open("GET", "news.asp", true);
req.send(null);

Three things in there shaped a decade of code. The third argument to open is the async flag, and true meant your script carried on while the request was out. That one boolean is the A in Ajax. The callback fired on every state change, so everyone learned to test for the magic number 4; the W3C's first draft listed the states by name, and 4 was "Loaded". And the response came back two ways: as a string in responseText, or parsed into a document in responseXML if the server sent XML. Most people, most of the time, wanted the string.

Other browsers had no ActiveX, so they couldn't copy the component. They copied its interface instead and exposed it as a plain constructor, new XMLHttpRequest(), with Microsoft's method names and a spelling that capitalizes half an acronym. (Microsoft's own component was XMLHTTP, all capitals.) Wikipedia's history puts it in Mozilla's Gecko engine by 2002, in Safari 1.2 in 2004 and in Opera 8.0 in 2005. Aaron Swartz, looking back in A Brief History of Ajax, summed up those years: "Mozilla quickly followed suit and, while nobody I know used it, the function stayed there, just waiting to be taken advantage of."

Why it sat unused

Six years is a long time for a feature this useful to sit unused. I count four reasons, and I think they mattered in roughly this order.

It lived behind ActiveX. For the first few years the object existed in one browser on one operating system, behind the same mechanism that security-minded administrators were busy switching off. A public site that depended on it was betting on the visitor's browser and the visitor's IT department. Garrett, asked in a 2006 interview about the standards work then starting, said something that fits: people had tried to solve the problem "in proprietary ways for years", and the approach "didn't get traction until it was broadly available in a vendor-neutral way". The dates fit. Safari's support came in 2004, the year Gmail launched.

The timing was terrible. The object shipped in 1999 and the dot-com crash followed. Swartz's history has a bleak phrase for the period: "Shortly thereafter the bubble burst and web development crashed." The teams that might have spent 2001 building ambitious browser applications were mostly not employed to do so. Hopmann, explaining why the idea hadn't caught on even earlier, grants the slow connections and slow machines of the late 1990s ("typical machines were 200mhz") and then names what he thinks mattered most: developers don't make sweeping shifts quickly, and "these things take 3-5 years".

Nobody could see the examples. Outlook Web Access was the first big application built this way, and it lived behind corporate logins. Oddpost, a webmail service that opened in 2002 and behaved like a desktop mail client, charged a subscription, and Swartz reckons that is why it "didn't receive as much attention". Gmail launched on April 1, 2004, two and a half years after work on it began. Paul Buchheit recalls that along the way quite a few colleagues wanted it killed, or rebuilt with native client software, "not this crazy Javascript stuff". It was free, but its script was hard to follow. The breakthrough was the small one. Google Suggest appeared in December 2004, a search box that completed your query as you typed, and Hopmann notes that people "looked at the source code of that page to figure out how it worked". View Source was the school, and for once the lesson was short enough to read. Google Maps followed on February 8, 2005.

It had no name. Developers called it XMLHTTP, or remote scripting, or described it by pointing at Gmail. None of those fits on a slide. I think this reason is underrated, and the next section is my argument for it.

February 18, 2005

Ten days after Google Maps appeared, Jesse James Garrett of the San Francisco consultancy Adaptive Path published Ajax: A New Approach to Web Applications. Garrett was a user experience designer writing for other designers, and the essay reads that way. It has two diagrams and no code. The key sentences:

Google Suggest and Google Maps are two examples of a new approach to web applications that we at Adaptive Path have been calling Ajax. The name is shorthand for Asynchronous JavaScript + XML, and it represents a fundamental shift in what's possible on the Web.

Garrett was careful to say what the word covered: "Ajax isn't a technology. It's really several technologies", listed as XHTML and CSS, the DOM, XML and XSLT, XMLHttpRequest, and JavaScript "binding everything together". The essay claimed no invention. A follow-up Q&A three weeks later answered the obvious challenge directly: "Neither Adaptive Path nor Google invented Ajax." Asked why the thing needed a name at all, Garrett gave the most honest answer in the history of technical branding:

I needed something shorter than "Asynchronous JavaScript+CSS+DOM+XMLHttpRequest" to use when discussing this approach with clients.

In the 2006 interview Garrett filled in the scene. The technical people at a client already understood the pieces; the word was for "the business people I was dealing with". Then Garrett published the essay and "left the country", spending two weeks in Japan without internet access and coming home to "this avalanche of e-mail".

The speed of what followed is the evidence that the name was the missing part. On March 22, 2005, thirty-two days after the essay, Rails 0.11.0 shipped with the word in its release title and "Ajax helpers" as the headline feature. By the time Hopmann wrote his account, the term had reached the Wall Street Journal. Douglas Crockford, never one to oversell a trend, later described the moment this way: "In 2005, the idea of Dynamic HTML gained new energy and acceptance when it was renamed as Ajax."

Hopmann's verdict on his former employer is harsher than anything I'd write: "At Microsoft we totally blew the opportunity to evangelize and get out in front of this approach back in 1999."

Living with two constructors

Once everyone wanted to make requests, everyone needed the same few lines at the top of the file, because there were two ways to get the object. The canonical version is short enough that the Internet Explorer team published it themselves in January 2006:

if (window.XMLHttpRequest){
  // If IE7, Mozilla, Safari, etc: Use native object
  var xmlHttp = new XMLHttpRequest()
}
else
{
  if (window.ActiveXObject){
    // ...otherwise, use the ActiveX control for IE5.x and IE6
    var xmlHttp = new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
  }
}

Read the first comment again. That post, by program manager Sunava Dutta, was announcing that Internet Explorer 7 would support "a scriptable native version of XMLHTTP", so that organizations which had disabled ActiveX could still run these applications. Microsoft was adopting the other browsers' imitation of Microsoft's own component, and putting itself on the "native object" branch of a test that had existed only to route around it. Internet Explorer 7 shipped in October 2006. The else branch stayed in libraries for years, since Internet Explorer 6 did too.

Careful versions of that snippet grew a ladder of try blocks, asking for "Msxml2.XMLHTTP" first and falling back to "Microsoft.XMLHTTP", because the component had been reissued under more than one name. Nobody wanted to write that twice, so the wrapper became the first thing every library offered. Prototype, the library that grew up alongside Rails, reduced a request to:

new Ajax.Request('/some_url', {
  method:'get',
  onSuccess: function(transport) {
    var response = transport.responseText || "no response text";
    alert("Success! \n\n" + response);
  },
  onFailure: function() { alert('Something went wrong...'); }
});

No readyState, no magic 4, no ActiveX. jQuery later did the same with $.ajax, and I'd guess a large share of working developers went a decade without typing XMLHttpRequest at all. The word in the method name was Garrett's.

The X went quietly. Garrett's own Q&A had already conceded that you didn't need XML, and could use "a technology like JavaScript Object Notation". Parsing a responseXML document with DOM calls was miserable next to getting an object you could use directly, and by December 2006 Crockford could tell an XML conference, to its face, that "JSON has become the X in Ajax".

What it left behind

A standard written by transcription. The W3C published its first working draft of "The XMLHttpRequest Object" on April 5, 2006, seven years after the object shipped. Its stated method was to "document a minimum set of interoperable features based on existing implementations", and it adds that "only features that are already implemented are considered". It also acknowledges being derived from the WHATWG's work documenting existing behavior. So the chain runs: a Microsoft team writes a component for its own product, other browsers reverse-engineer the interface, a group of browser people writes down what the copies do, and the standards body publishes that. I don't mean this as a complaint. It is how most of the platform you rely on got specified, and this is one of the cleanest examples.

A name nobody can fix. The current living standard carries a sentence I find oddly moving: "The name XMLHttpRequest is historical and has no bearing on its functionality." It was true the weekend the thing was written. The XML was a shipping excuse from the start, and the web will carry it for as long as there is a web, capital letters and all.

The synchronous flag outlived its reason. Hopmann's first version "didn't have async support hooked up", so the blocking mode came first and the famous one was added in the rewrite. A blocking request freezes the page while it waits, and browsers have been trying to remove it for years. The spec says synchronous requests outside of workers are "in the process of being removed from the web platform", and then adds, in brackets, "This is a long process that takes many years." A blocking mode from a weekend prototype is still being negotiated a quarter of a century later.

The engine in the diagram became the framework. Garrett's essay describes the browser loading "an Ajax engine", written in JavaScript, that is "responsible for both rendering the interface the user sees and communicating with the server on the user's behalf". In 2005 that was a box in a figure. It is also a fair description of what a single-page application framework does, written years before the big ones existed. The problems arrived with it. Garrett's Q&A lists, as open questions, accessibility, the back button, and what happens when JavaScript is off, and answers all of them with "maybe". The industry spent the next fifteen years turning those maybes into routers, history APIs and server rendering.

The security review came later. The rule browsers settled on was that a page could call only its own server, and the 2006 draft gives it one line: "Same-origin security restrictions SHOULD apply." Everything developers then wanted, calling other people's servers, needed a new permission system, which is where the 2008 Level 2 draft's "cross-site requests" and the CORS errors in your console come from. The "quick security review" of the late 1990s has been followed by a rather longer one.

The replacement, fetch, arrived in the mid-2010s, and MDN describes it as "a more powerful and flexible replacement for XMLHttpRequest". It returns a promise instead of counting to 4. The old constructor is still in every browser, and a great deal of code still calls it through one wrapper or another.

The takeaway

The capability and the name are different inventions, and the web needed both. Microsoft shipped the capability in 1999, for one product, under a name chosen to get it past a release deadline. It worked. Hardly anyone outside noticed, because it was locked to one browser, because the industry was in a slump, because the best examples were hidden behind logins and paywalls, and because nobody could say in a meeting what it was. Each of those took years to clear, and the last one was cleared in an afternoon's reading by a designer who had written no part of the code.

I'd argue that makes Garrett's essay a piece of engineering in its own right. Hopmann, who built the first version, came to the same view: "effective marketing and communication of your ideas is important and we missed out on that." A feature that can't be named can't be asked for, budgeted, taught or put in a job ad. The object had one name that was wrong from its first day and survived anyway; the technique had none for six years and stayed obscure until it got one.

item.title: Firebug: the first look inside the page
item.description: In January 2006 one developer uploaded a few days of code as a Firefox add-on, and within a few years every browser had copied its panels, its F12 key and its console.log.
item.content:encoded:
The tool that showed every browser what developer tools should be was an add-on, uploaded when it was a few days old, and nearly sold for the price of a paperback.

This is a very early release – the code is only a few days old. Beware of the leopard.

That is the note Joe Hewitt attached to Firebug 0.2 when it went up on Mozilla's add-ons site in January 2006, as quoted by Jan "Honza" Odvarko in Mozilla's farewell to the project eleven years later. The leopard is borrowed from Douglas Adams, where it is the sign on the door of the room, down in a cellar, in which some planning documents are officially "on display." It is a decent joke for a tool whose whole job was to show you things that had been kept in the basement.

Version 0.2 did not look like the start of anything. It was one panel inside the Firefox window. But by the time the extension stopped working in November 2017, every major browser shipped tools built to the same plan, the F12 key opened most of them, and the function it had taught pages to call was a web standard.

Before: alert() and five separate tools

The standard debugging technique of the early 2000s was alert(). The people who built the replacements say so themselves. The WebKit team's ten-year retrospective calls the period "the wild west of web development, when your best debugging aid was alert()." John J. Barton, who later led Firebug from inside IBM, remembered enterprise web apps starting to grow "without much more than 'window.alert()' debugging." You put a dialog box where you wanted a breakpoint and clicked OK until the loop ran out.

Tools did exist. They just lived apart. View Source showed the HTML the server had sent, which was less and less like the page in front of you once scripts started rewriting it. Mozilla shipped a DOM Inspector that showed the live tree. Mozilla also had Venkman, a real JavaScript debugger with breakpoints, stepping, a call stack and a profiler. A commenter under the Mozilla farewell, Alvaro G. Vicario, summed up its reputation kindly: "It was surely great, but I could never figure out how to use it." And there was the browser's JavaScript Console, a list of errors, improved by an extension called Console2.

Mike Ratcliffe's history of Firebug, written in 2013 and drawing on Hewitt's own account, names the tools that Firebug's features were inspired by: Venkman for the debugger, Console2 for error reporting, an extension called View Source Chart for the HTML tree, the Aardvark extension for pointing at an element with the mouse, and the interactive interpreter that came with the MochiKit library for the command line. So every part of Firebug existed in 2005, spread across five separate projects.

The author was unusually well placed to notice. Hewitt had worked on the Netscape user interface, was one of the small group that started the stripped-down browser that became Firefox, and had written the DOM Inspector himself. Then, in Ratcliffe's telling, he went back to building websites and "soon found that the state of the art tools that he had used as a web developer in the late 90s had not changed."

Twelve months, from one panel to 1.0

The first release was that single panel. According to Ratcliffe it was "roughly equivalent to the console panel," it logged Ajax requests as they happened, and the way for a page to write a message into it was a function called printfire. Jay Hoffmann's history of web debugging dates Hewitt's announcement to January 12, 2006. I could not open Hewitt's own post from the period, so hold the day loosely. The month is solid, although the opening paragraph of Odvarko's farewell says 2005 and its own timeline says otherwise.

Here is the coincidence I like best in this story. On January 15, 2006, a first version of a tool called Web Inspector landed in the WebKit source, and Timothy Hatcher introduced it the next day. It let you "browse the live DOM hierarchy" and listed the CSS rules that applied to a node "with overridden properties striked-out." Two browser people reached for the same missing tool in the same fortnight, from opposite ends. Web Inspector began with the tree and the styles and, by WebKit's later admission, "didn't even have a console." Firebug began as a console and not much else.

Firebug then grew at a pace that only a one-person project manages. Version 0.3 added an inspector tab with the HTML tree. On April 25, 2006, John Resig told readers that Hewitt wanted testers for a JavaScript debugger. The link in that post goes to a page on Hewitt's site whose file name is goodbye_venkman.php. Version 0.4 shipped the debugger in May, and Ratcliffe records the other change in that release in one line: console.log, console.warn, console.info and the rest "replaced printfire and were made available to all web pages."

That sentence is where a browser add-on began defining an API for the web. Here is the start of the function that defines it, as it stood in the Firebug 1.1 source tree, which carries Hewitt's name as creator and is still browsable on a third-party mirror:

function FirebugConsole(context, win)
{
    this.firebug = Firebug.version;

    // We store these functions as closures so that they can access the context privately,
    // because it would be insecure to store context as a property of window.console and
    // and therefore expose it to web pages.

    this.log = function()
    {
        logFormatted(arguments, "log");
    };

On May 30, 2006, Jesse Skinner wrote: "The days of using alert() for debugging are over (except, perhaps, in other browsers." The closing bracket never arrived, and the exception in the brackets turned out to matter. I'll come back to it.

The 1.0 beta was out by the first week of December 2006. Ratcliffe describes version 1.0 as "a complete redesign of the Firebug user interface from the ground up," and lists what was new, including CSS editing, network load timing, box model visualization, JavaScript profiling, command line autocomplete, DOM editing, a separate window. Simon Willison's link log for December 4 reads, in full: "Unbelievably brilliant software. I use this every day." Three days later Roger Johansson compared it with the Web Inspector in the WebKit nightlies, which "honestly pales in comparison."

It almost had a price tag. Hewitt had decided people depended on Firebug for their jobs and that it needed full-time work. Ratcliffe says he was "considering making it a paid product ($15 - $25) so that he could employ a couple of full-time engineers." Hewitt floated the idea on his blog, and by his own account the response was encouraging. Then, in December, he announced the opposite. The passage is quoted in the Mozilla farewell:

However, in the end, I just don't feel like that is the right thing to do. I love working on Firebug because I know I'm making a lot of people happy and helping to advance the state of the art. That's a lot more meaningful to me than just about anything else, and so, I've decided that Firebug will remain free and open source.

Firebug 1.0 final followed in January 2007, a year after the leopard.

Why this one caught on

None of the parts were new, so the explanation has to be somewhere else. Here are the forces I'd point to.

It was one tool, attached to the page. Hoffmann's verdict on Firebug and Web Inspector is that "their largest advantage was that they combined everything into a single package." You pointed at an element in the page and landed on its node in the tree, with the CSS rules that applied to it alongside. From version 0.4 an error in the console came with a stack trace, and the same extension could stop the script. Once the tools were joined, a question about the page could be followed across all of them without starting again.

The page had started moving. By 2006 pages were turning into programs that changed after they loaded and talked to the server without telling you, and View Source could see none of it. Firebug logged XMLHttpRequest traffic from its first release, while the word Ajax was still new. Barton later wrote that Firebug arrived "at the start of the Web 2.0 revolution" and "helped shift people from thinking Web 2.0 was a fad to realizing Web apps can be real." I'd put it more plainly. An application whose state you cannot inspect is hard to treat as engineering.

The browser let one person ship it. Firebug was a Firefox extension, written in JavaScript, CSS and Mozilla's XUL markup, with the run of the browser's internals. Nobody at Mozilla had to approve it, schedule it or staff it. Distribution came with the platform too. In a 2007 interview for FOSDEM, Hewitt said that on the day Mozilla added Firebug to its list of recommended extensions, "downloads more than quadrupled and have not dropped since."

It was free on purpose. In the same interview Hewitt gave his reasons without much ceremony: "The state of web development tools is awful, and the quality of the web itself reflects that. I like money as much as the next guy, but what I really want is a more usable, better performing web." A $20 debugger would have found customers. I doubt every tutorial would have assumed you had it.

Libraries and companies built on it. Hewitt told FOSDEM that "many of the popular JavaScript frameworks like Dojo, jQuery, YUI, and MochiKit use Firebug's logging feature for their built-in debugging facilities." In May 2007 Willison linked a YUI team announcement, headed "The YUI Team Is Hiring an Engineer To Work on Firebug," and quoted it: "we're opening a search for a full-time developer to work with Joe on advancing the Firebug roadmap." That July Yahoo's performance team released YSlow, which Willison described as "an extension on top of another extension." Once other people's tools assumed Firebug, it was infrastructure.

Living with it

The first problem was the one in Skinner's brackets. console.log worked where Firebug was installed. Anywhere else, a logging call you forgot to delete reached for an object that did not exist, threw an error and took the rest of your script with it. Hewitt's answer was Firebug Lite, which Willison linked on the same day as the 1.0 beta: "Add Firebug to your site for non-Firefox browsers." In the same folder of the source tree sits a second, much smaller file, called firebugx.js. This is all of it:

if (!window.console || !console.firebug)
{
    var names = ["log", "debug", "info", "warn", "error", "assert", "dir", "dirxml",
    "group", "groupEnd", "time", "timeEnd", "count", "trace", "profile", "profileEnd"];

    window.console = {};
    for (var i = 0; i < names.length; ++i)
        window.console[names[i]] = function() {}
}

Sixteen functions that do nothing, so that a page full of debugging statements could run where there was no Firebug to receive them. The test on the first line reads the firebug property that FirebugConsole sets in the earlier listing. If the console in front of it was not Firebug's, the stub replaced it.

The second problem was the author. Parakey, the startup Hewitt had co-founded with Blake Ross, was bought by Facebook in July 2007, and he went with it. Firebug at that point was very largely one person's code. A year later Resig laid out the state of things with some candour. There were "approximately, three developers who've done any sort of serious bug fixing on the internals," across "some 35,000 lines of JavaScript code." The original author was "quite incommunicado these days." Testing was "quite abysmal," to the point that "features have gotten accidentally removed from releases simply because they weren't immediately apparent that they existed."

What kept it alive was an odd coalition. Odvarko started working on Firebug in 2007, beginning with the Net panel, and once Odvarko was on board IBM agreed to support Barton's work on it. Mozilla put Resig and Rob Campbell on a Firebug team, and a Firebug Working Group met, in Resig's account, at Google. Barton later wrote that Firebug 1.1 "wasn't really meant to be," which made 1.2, in August 2008, the first real release beyond Hewitt's code. The licence files record the handover. The one in the 1.1 tree reads "Copyright (c) 2007, Parakey Inc." Its successor in the final repository reads "Copyright (c) 2009, Mozilla Foundation."

Meanwhile the other browsers were taking notes. WebKit's 2007 redesign of Web Inspector added a console "with live JavaScript evaluation" and a network panel with a load timeline. Opera's Dragonfly was out in alpha by May 2008, and Willison's summary was "Opera's new Firebug-style developer console." Microsoft had a developer toolbar for Internet Explorer 6 and 7, and built the tools into the browser from version 8. And in September 2008 the WebKit blog reported that "our compatibility with Firebug's command line and window.console APIs has also been greatly improved" by Keishi Hattori, a University of Tokyo student, "as a summer project." A browser engine was now treating an extension for a rival browser as the specification to conform to.

The end was slow and fairly gracious. Mozilla decided to build developer tools into Firefox, and, as Odvarko wrote, "the decision was made not to use Firebug as the platform to build upon." Firefox 10, in January 2012, shipped an "Inspect tool with content highlighting." Firebug 2.0 came out in June 2014, and after that the team was "in maintenance mode." The last version was 2.0.19. Then Firefox 57, on November 14, 2017, stopped running the old kind of extension altogether. Odvarko, by then on the Firefox DevTools team, wrote that "more than a million loyal fans" were still using Firebug that autumn.

What it left behind

A standard nobody designed. There is now a WHATWG Console Standard. Fourteen of the sixteen names in firebugx.js are in it, every one except profile and profileEnd, along with the %o and %s format specifiers. The standard is frank about being written after the fact. A note says that "for historical reasons, console is lowercased," the namespace object gets a special rule "for historical web-compatibility reasons," and the part that puts text on the screen is left "implementation-defined." Its status section still calls it "an early work in progress" and "the editors' first specification." I ran the sixteen names through a current Chromium while writing this, and all sixteen are still functions, the two unstandardized ones included. So the most-typed debugging API on the web began in a 0.4 release of a browser add-on and was written down by a standards body years later. It is the route Microsoft's innerHTML took, ship first and specify later, except that this time the proprietary vendor was one person.

The dollar sign in your console changed sides. Type $('nav') into a console today and you get the page's first nav element back, with no library loaded. That is Firebug's Command Line API, still in service. Here is how it looked in the 1.1 source:

this.$ = function(id)
{
    var doc = baseWindow.document;
    return baseWindow.document.getElementById(id);
};

this.$$ = function(selector)
{
    return FBL.getElementsBySelector(baseWindow.document, selector);
};

In Firebug, $ took an ID. That was Prototype's meaning of the dollar sign, the one jQuery had to step around. Chrome's Console Utilities now document $(selector) as "a shortcut for the document.querySelector() function," which is jQuery's meaning. The console quietly followed the library that won. The rest of the list barely moved. The 1.1 file defines nineteen commands, among them $$, $x, inspect, keys, values, copy, monitor and monitorEvents, and Chrome's page documents every one of them except cd.

The file you send to support. The Firebug team wanted a way to export what Odvarko's Net panel had captured. Steve Souders, in the Firebug Working Group, suggested in 2009 that "rather than create yet another proprietary format, Firebug team up with HttpWatch to develop a common format." By Souders's own account, the name was Souders's contribution: HAR. Chrome's Network panel documents an "Export HAR" button today, and every support desk that asks you to "attach a HAR file" is asking for a format first shipped in HttpWatch and in a Firebug add-on called NetExport.

Breakpoints on things that are not lines. Stopping when a request fires, or when a DOM node changes, feels as if it had always been there. Barton and Odvarko wrote those up for Firebug 1.5 as "Dynamic and Graphical Web Page Breakpoints" and submitted the paper to the WWW 2010 conference. Odvarko wrote later that "you might know these features as Break on XHR, Break on Next, Break on DOM mutation, etc." The same goes for the F12 key. Wikipedia's article on Firebug traces it to the 0.2.3 release of January 31, 2006, and Firefox's migration guide says simply that the built-in tools "share the same shortcuts."

It replaced View Source just as View Source went dark. The years in which Firebug spread are the years in which minifiers and build steps made the source of a page unreadable. Reading other people's pages did not stop. It moved from the file the server sent to the live tree, where an element could be picked with the mouse and its styles switched off one at a time. I'd argue "Inspect Element" is a better teacher than the menu item it displaced, because you can change things and watch what happens. Willison's note on the farewell goes further: "It's hard to overstate how influential Firebug has been in helping to turn front-end web development into a respected and productive engineering discipline."

The platform that made it possible is gone. Firebug could exist because a 2006 Firefox extension could reach into anything. Firefox 57 "exclusively supports extensions built using the WebExtension API," and as far as I can see that API could not host a second Firebug. Today a browser's debugger comes from the browser's vendor. Hewitt had seen where the value was. Asked in 2007 about a Firebug 2.0, he said that "the theme of the next version will be extensibility," with pages adding "their own tabs and buttons."

The takeaway

Firebug did not invent the DOM tree view, the JavaScript debugger, the error console or the command line. Each of those existed, in its own window, with its own author. What Hewitt did in January 2006 was put them in one panel under the page and connect them, at the moment pages turned into programs, and in the same fortnight that another browser engine began building the same thing in-house. He then gave the result away, which is why it became the common language rather than a product. Within a few years every major browser had its own version, and at least one of them was describing its work as compatibility with Firebug.

The extension is dead and almost everything it defined is alive. console.log is a standard, $ and $$ answer in every console, HAR files cross every support desk, and F12 still opens the tools in most browsers. The farewell page at getfirebug.com says the work "lives on in Firefox Developer Tools." That is true, and it is also too modest. It lives on in all of them, mostly under the names a few days of code gave it.

item.title: View Source was the school
item.description: For about fifteen years the web trained its own workforce through one menu item that showed how any page was made, and then the pages stopped being readable.
item.content:encoded:
The web's training programme was a menu item that nobody was required to ship. It taught a generation of developers, and then the lessons got harder to read.

<!-- Badda Bing, Badda Boom -->

That is line 17 of the home page of the Space Jam website, which Warner Bros. still serves at spacejam.com/1996/. I fetched it on November 12, 2026 and the comment was there, eight lines below another one that reads "Copyright 1996 Warner Bros. Online". No visitor to the site was ever shown it. Every visitor could read it anyway, by picking one item from a menu.

The item was called View Source, or Document Source, or Page Source, depending on the browser and the year. It opened the file the server had sent, exactly as sent, comments and all. For a long stretch of the web's history that menu item was the nearest thing the trade had to a school. It had no teachers, no syllabus and no admissions office. This post is about how it got there, why it worked so well, who tried to switch it off, and what has replaced it.

Before: software arrived sealed

In the early 1990s, if you admired how a program worked, admiration was as far as you could go. Software shipped compiled. You could see what it did and not how. Building anything interactive meant buying a tool and learning its language first. Clay Shirky, looking back from 1998, put it this way: "Prior to the invention of HTML, all software packages which implemented any sort of hypertext required the user to learn a programming language of some sort (Director, Hypercard)."

The web's own first files were not written to be read either. Here is the top of the project's home page, from a copy CERN still serves:

<HEADER>
<TITLE>The World Wide Web project</TITLE>
<NEXTID N="55">
</HEADER>
<BODY>
<H1>World Wide Web</H1>The WorldWideWeb (W3) is a wide-area<A
NAME=0 HREF="WhatIs.html">
hypermedia</A> information retrieval

The line breaks fall in the middle of tags, and no person typing by hand would put them there. And NEXTID is a note from a program to itself. The HTML 2.0 specification later described it as "a hint for the name to use for a new <A> element when editing an HTML document", included "for historical reasons only". An editor wrote this file and left itself a counter for the next link.

That editor was Tim Berners-Lee's first browser, which could write pages as well as show them. His FAQ page describes it as "a graphical point-and-click browser with mode-free editing and link creation", and captions a screenshot of himself making a link with some pride: "Look - no typing URLS, no <angle brackets>!" My reading is that the markup was meant to be a file format, like the insides of a word processor document. People were supposed to work above it.

The browsers that spread the web did not keep the editing half. They kept a window onto the raw file. That turned out to matter more.

What happened: one menu item

The user's guide for NCSA Mosaic 2.4 lists the File menu: New Window, Clone Window, Open URL, Reload Current, and, further down, this.

View Source... (hotkey d)
    Pop up a dialog box showing you the current
    document's Uniform Resource Locator and
    HTML source text.

It sits between "Find In Current" and "Save As", with nothing to mark it as important. Tim O'Reilly later traced the lineage: "The 'View Source' menu item migrated from Tim Berners-Lee's original browser, to Mosaic, and then on to Netscape Navigator and even Microsoft's Internet Explorer."

Internet Explorer added a twist of its own, apparently without meaning to. It had no source viewer, so it handed the file to a program that was already on the machine. A Microsoft blog post from 2008 admits as much: "Since the very beginning, IE has relied on the built-in Notepad editor to show page source. Notepad, it should be noted is not a source viewer." Quite so. Notepad is an editor. On Windows, then, View Source opened the page in a program with a Save As command. You were one menu away from owning a copy, and two keystrokes away from changing it.

So what did the school teach? Go back to Space Jam. A few lines under the comments is this:

<body bgcolor="#000000" background="img/bg_stars.gif" text="#ff0000" link="#ff4c4c" vlink="#ff4c4c" alink="#ff4c4c">

One line, and a newcomer in 1996 learns that pages have a background colour, that a background can be a tiled image, and that links have three states with a colour each. No book is needed. You change #000000 to something else, save, reload, and find out what the number meant. Further down, the planets on the famous star map turn out to be cells in a table:

<td align=center valign=middle>
<a href="cmp/jamcentral/jamcentralframes.html"><img src="img/p-jamcentral.gif" height=67 width=55 alt="Jam Central" border=0></a>
</td>

That is how layout was done, and the source is also how everybody found out. Shirky uses tables as his example of a tool escaping its purpose. They were "originally imagined to be just that – a tool for presenting tabular data", and their adoption "as the basic method for page layout did not have to be explicit in the design of either HTML or the browser". No specification told designers to do it and no vendor ran a course. One person worked it out, and everyone else read their source.

When scripting arrived the same thing happened to JavaScript, because early scripts sat in the page between <script> tags. The command that taught you bgcolor taught you onmouseover as well.

The first person I can find who said clearly that this was the important part was Shirky, in an essay first published in April 1998 called "View Source… Lessons from the Web's Massively Parallel Development". Its subtitle is "The Web considered as a massive Open Source project." The core of it is one paragraph:

The single factor most responsible for this riot of experimentation is transparency – the ability of any user to render into source code the choices made by any other designer.

He adds that when a page is worth copying, "the question 'How did they do that?' can be answered in seconds." And he notes how easily it could have gone the other way. The first browser makers could have treated the feature "as a kind of debugging option which could have been disabled in any public release". They left it in.

Why it worked

Other platforms have let you read their source. Few of them trained a workforce by accident. Here are the forces I think made the difference. Reasonable people weigh them differently.

The format was text, and nothing stood between the text and the result. There was no compiler and no build. Alex Russell wrote in 2010 that web developers "get started by taking some code, pasting it into a file, saving, loading it in a browser and hitting ctrl-r." He called this the "copy-paste-tweak loop" and listed its kit: "The only required equipment is a text editor and a web browser, tools that are free and work together instantly." Shirky's version is that the web "removed the need for either compiling the results or seeking permission, certifcation or registration from anyone else." Both halves of that sentence count. You needed no tools and you needed no one's leave.

The browser forgave you. Copied fragments rarely fit. You pasted half a table into the wrong place, left a tag open, and the page rendered anyway, perhaps oddly. Russell again: "Browsers recovering from errors gracefully create a welcome learning environment, free of the inadequacy that a compile failure tends to evoke." A language that halts on the first mistake teaches you that you are wrong. A browser that shows you a lopsided page shows you how you are wrong, which is far more useful to a beginner at eleven at night.

The interface lived in the page. This is Shirky's subtlest point and I think his best. In most software the interface is part of the program. On the web, he wrote, an interface "can be integrated with the information it is displaying, instead of with the display software itself." So every page carried a complete, working design with it. There was always something worth copying, because the page was the whole product. Had browsers supplied the navigation bars and layouts themselves, View Source would have shown you a list of facts.

Nobody had to choose to share. This is the force that gets the least credit. Russell is blunt about it: "view source is nearly never locally beneficial." No company gains from showing its competitors how its home page is built. He had lost count of the times he had seen "the 'how do I hide my code?' question" from newcomers. If transparency had been a checkbox, most commercial sites would have left it unticked. It was a property of the medium, and so the question never came up. O'Reilly made the same observation about a different product. Napster grew because its defaults shared whatever you downloaded, and systems like that let "users pursuing their own 'selfish' interests build collective value as an automatic byproduct." View Source was sharing set as the default, with no setting to change.

There was not yet much to protect. Shirky describes the early web as having "no discernible financial incentive for the majority of its initial participants." A band page and a list of favourite links are not trade secrets. By the time there was real money in a page's markup, the habit of reading each other's work was already the culture, and the people who had learned that way were the ones being hired.

Living with it: the people who wanted it off

Not everyone enjoyed being the textbook. Photographers, designers and small businesses saw their pictures and layouts turn up on other people's sites, and wanted a lock. The lock they got was the no-right-click script. This one is from the irt.org JavaScript FAQ, question 969, "How can I suppress a right mouse click?":

<script language="JavaScript1.1"><!--
var debug = true;
function right(e) {
  if (navigator.appName == 'Netscape' && (e.which == 3 || e.which == 2)) return false;
  else if (navigator.appName == 'Microsoft Internet Explorer' && (event.button == 2 || event.button == 3)) {
    alert('Denied!');
    return false;
  }

  return true;
}
document.onmousedown=right;
if (document.layers) window.captureEvents(Event.MOUSEDOWN);
window.onmousedown=right;
//--></script>

It is a fine period piece: browser sniffing by name, a document.layers check, and an alert box that says "Denied!". What I like most is the FAQ's own commentary, which talks the reader out of the script before presenting it. "This script is not fool-proof," it begins. It "doesn't stop users browsing the source of youe page from the toolbar menus." And then the advice that has not aged a day: if the script does not do what you need, "then don't use it and don't put your images/scripts on the net." If your living depends on your images, add a watermark.

The scripts spread regardless, and how they spread is the joke. A Firefox bug report from 2004, titled "Javascript can disable right click", quotes the offending code from the page in question. Its first two lines are a credit: "Disable right click script III- By Renigade", and "For full source code, visit http://www.dynamicdrive.com". The reporter presumably got those lines by reading the page's source. The anti-copying script was distributed by being copied, and it was attributed because the copyists kept the comment.

The thing that did close the book was never meant as a lock. Douglas Crockford's JSMin, which he dates to 2001, "removes comments and unnecessary whitespace from JavaScript files" to make them download faster. He is careful about what it is: "JSMin does not obfuscate, but it does uglify." And he is honest about the price: "The result may be harder to debug. It will definitely be harder to read."

Minified code could still be puzzled out with patience. Compiled code could not. On November 5, 2009 Google open-sourced the Closure Compiler, which it had built for its own web applications. Four months later, after a conference panel on this exact subject, Russell wrote a follow-up. Someone on the panel had pointed out that beautifiers could tidy minified code. Russell replied that a compiler which inlines functions, removes dead code and moves the rest around is a different animal. The output was "much, much smaller than I can wring out by hand" and also "totally unrecognizable." His conclusion was that JavaScript treated this way is "functionally indistinguishable from a bytecode format like SWF or Java", with the same effect on learning: "less ability to easily share techniques, a smaller group of more professional users, and a heavier reliance on tooling."

Nobody set out to end the lesson. Pages got heavy, bytes cost money, and the fix for bytes was to remove everything a human reader needed.

What it left behind

The fix Russell asked for got built, and the default flipped. In that follow-up he said compiled JavaScript would need "brand new tools akin to symbol servers" to be workable. The seed already existed. The same Closure announcement mentions Closure Inspector, "a Firebug extension that makes debugging the obfuscated code almost as easy as debugging the human-readable source." The source map specification says its first format "was created by Joseph Schorr for use by Closure Inspector". That format went through two more revisions, and in December 2024 it became ECMA-426, an Ecma standard for mapping shipped code back to what a person wrote. So readable source came back as a file you may publish beside your code if you choose to. In 1996 you had to do nothing to be readable. Now you have to do something, and you may just as reasonably keep the map private for your own error reports. I'd argue that switch, from on by default to off by default, changed more than any single tool did.

The source stopped being the page. Browsers now offer two commands that sound alike and do different jobs. Chrome's documentation spells out the gap: "HTML represents initial page content and the DOM represents active, current page content. When JavaScript adds, removes, or edits nodes, the DOM becomes different than the HTML." On Space Jam the two are the same thing, so View Source tells you everything. On a page built in the browser by a script, View Source shows the instructions for fetching a program, and the inspector shows a result with no record of how it got that way. Neither is what a learner in 1996 had, which was the author's own file.

The folk feature was ratified late, and on thin paperwork. You can still type view-source: in front of an address. That prefix was registered with IANA as a URI scheme on May 25, 2011, with the status "Provisional". By then it was a habit of very long standing. For its list of implementations the registration refers readers to "Wikipedia's entry on 'View-source URI scheme'". It also carries a quiet legal caution that the source "might sometimes refer to source code that is under certain legal provisions, which might not grant free access". That is the old copy-and-paste question, raised in a standards registry fifteen years after Warner Bros. put a copyright notice in a comment and then served the comment to everyone.

The command survived, and it grew a red pen. View Source is still Ctrl+U in Firefox, and Firefox's documentation lists what it has learned since: line numbers you can link to, and syntax highlighting that "also highlights parsing errors in red." The forgiving parser still renders your mistakes, and the viewer next to it now marks them, so the school has acquired a teacher after all. Russell noted in 2010 that the inspectors grew from the same root. Firebug and its descendants allow "live changes without reloads, even on pages you don't 'own'." Firebug gets its own post here soon.

The phrase outlived the practice. When Mozilla started a conference for front-end developers in 2015, held in Portland that November, it named the event View Source. By then the two words stood for a whole account of how the web was meant to work, one that Shirky had written down in 1998. One of his rules deserves a wider audience: "Good tools allow users to do stupid things." A tool that prevents mistakes, he argued, raises quality in the short run and "ultimately hampers development by not letting users learn from their mistakes." A great deal of modern tooling exists to stop you shipping a mistake. I think that is usually right for the product. I am less sure it is right for the person, and View Source was the last major teaching tool that didn't care.

Where is the school now? My best guess is that it moved to places where sharing is a decision: public repositories, documentation, tutorials and other people's answers to questions. There is more to read than there ever was, and it is better organised. The difference is that everything in it was put there on purpose, by someone who thought it was fit to be seen. The old school showed you the production code of a film studio, including the comment somebody left in for a laugh.

The takeaway

View Source worked as a school because of a coincidence of four things: a text format, an interpreter with no build step, a parser that forgave errors, and a default nobody could opt out of. Take away any one and you get something lesser. The last is the one we lost, and nobody took it. It went as a side effect of making pages faster, one removed comment at a time, until the file the server sent was no longer the file anyone wrote.

What replaced it is in many ways better: open repositories, real debuggers, and a standard for mapping shipped code back to its source. But it is all opt-in, and opt-in transparency teaches you what people are willing to show. The old kind taught you what they actually did. This page, for what it's worth, has no build step. The command still works here.

item.title: jQuery 1.0: what $ really replaced
item.description: jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006 with a dollar sign borrowed from another library, and replaced a folder of copy-pasted fixes that its own author had been winning contests with.
item.content:encoded:
The dollar sign was second-hand, the best ideas were credited to other people, and the browsers spent the next decade copying it anyway.

if ( $ )
  jQuery._$ = $;

var $ = jQuery;

Those lines sit about sixty lines into the file jQuery's CDN still serves as jquery-1.0.js. The last one is the famous one. The first two are more interesting, and the comment above them in the source says what they are for: "Map over the $ in case of overwrite." Before jQuery takes the dollar sign, it checks whether somebody else is already using it, and puts theirs somewhere safe.

Somebody else was. By 2006 $ already meant something on a lot of pages, and it meant something different. So the question in the title has two answers. The dollar sign replaced another library's dollar sign. And jQuery, the thing behind it, replaced a folder of small functions that every working developer carried from job to job, a few of which the author of jQuery had personally written.

jQuery 1.0 was announced on August 26, 2006. To see what it changed, start a year earlier.

Before: the utility belt

In 2005 the DOM worked, more or less, in every browser that mattered. The trouble was that it worked differently in each, and the standard way of doing things was long-winded even where it worked. You fetched one element with document.getElementById, or a list with getElementsByTagName, and then you looped. Attaching a click handler meant addEventListener in Mozilla, Opera and Safari, and attachEvent in Internet Explorer, which also forgot which element the handler belonged to.

Nobody wrote this out fresh each time. You had a file, often called something like common.js, with an addEvent(), a function to find elements by class name, something to run code when the page loaded, and a wrapper to create an XMLHttpRequest. Each function had an author and a URL in a comment, and each had known bugs.

The state of the art is nicely preserved on QuirksMode. On September 8, 2005, Peter-Paul Koch launched a contest to rewrite addEvent(), because the version everyone had been pasting "doesn't quite cut the cake any more." The judges were Koch, Scott Andrew LePera and Dean Edwards. The prize was "eternal and undying fame," plus a promise to "spread the winning entry as the new standard." Entries had to work in "Explorer 5+ Windows, Mozilla, Opera, and Safari."

That contest shows how the web platform got patched in 2005. There was no package manager and no committee. A respected blogger held a competition, and the winning snippet was distributed by copy and paste. The winner was announced on October 18, and here it is, as edited by the judges:

function addEvent( obj, type, fn )
{
  if (obj.addEventListener)
    obj.addEventListener( type, fn, false );
  else if (obj.attachEvent)
  {
    obj["e"+type+fn] = fn;
    obj[type+fn] = function() { obj["e"+type+fn]( window.event ); }
    obj.attachEvent( "on"+type, obj[type+fn] );
  }
}

The three lines in the attachEvent branch exist to make this work. As the author's own write-up put it, in Internet Explorer "the 'this' reference refers to the worthless 'window', when, in fact, it should refer to the parent object." The trick is to store the handler as a property of the element, keyed by the event type plus the function's entire source text, and call it from there. Koch wrote that "by far the most important reason" for the choice was "its brevity."

The winner was John Resig, born in 1984 and so 21 at the time. His entry is still linked from his site, at a path under /apps/jselect/. Remember that folder name.

Two other pieces of the belt matter here. In March 2003 Simon Willison had published document.getElementsBySelector, "a javascript function which takes a standard CSS style selector and returns an array of elements objects." His example was document.getElementsBySelector('div#main p a.external'). And Sam Stephenson's Prototype library had a function called $. Its documentation still calls it "the cornerstone of Prototype" and "a handy alias for document.getElementById." In Prototype, $('nav') hands you one element, by ID.

What happened

On August 22, 2005, two and a half weeks before the contest opened, Resig posted "Selectors in Javascript". It was a reaction to a library called Behaviour, which let you attach functions to elements using CSS selectors. He liked the premise and disliked the typing. Behaviour, he wrote, "simply seems too tedious and verbose for everyday use." Here is its way of making list items delete themselves when clicked, quoted from the post:

Behaviour.register({
  '#example li': function(e){
    e.onclick = function(){
      this.parentNode.removeChild(this);
    }
  }
});

And here is what Resig called "the same as above, done in my code":

$('#example li').bind('click',function(){
  this.parentNode.removeChild(this);
});

There was no code behind it yet. He called it "a syntactical mock-up." What the post did have was a measurement. Under the heading "Syntactic fluff comparision" he stripped both versions down to the characters that carry no meaning:

A: Behaviour.register({'':function(e){e.on=}});
B: $('').bind('',);

I think that is the most important artifact in the whole story. The API was designed by counting keystrokes that were not the selector, the event name or the function. Everything left over was a cost. A third sample in the same post chained calls together, with .set(), .bind() and .style() one after another on the same selection. The whole shape of jQuery is there in August 2005, a year before 1.0.

The first release came at BarCamp NYC in January 2006. The jQuery project dates it to January 14, the Saturday. Resig's own wrap-up, posted on the 16th, lists his demo slot as "11am, Sunday," so take your pick. It was the third thing he showed in that slot, after two web apps. He announced it as "jQuery: New Wave Javascript" and added, with the confidence of someone who has not yet had to maintain it, "this code revolutionizes the way you can get Javascript to interact with HTML."

Three days later a commenter named Kris De Volder pointed out that he already ran a project called JQuery, a Java code browser. Resig's reply explains the folder name from the contest: "I was, originally, going to use JSelect, but all the domain names were taken already."

In 2015 Resig dug up that January 2006 code and put it online with annotations. It opens like this:

function $(a,c) {
  if ( a == null ) return;

  // Since we're using Prototype's $ function,
  // be nice and have backwards compatability
  if ( typeof Prototype != "undefined" && a.constructor == String ) {

So the original jQuery had no jQuery function at all. The library was a function named $, and its comment says outright whose name that was. If Prototype was on the page and you passed a plain word, it tried getElementById first, so old Prototype code kept working. By 1.0 the real name had become jQuery, $ was an alias, and the previous owner's $ was parked in jQuery._$. That is the snippet at the top of this essay.

The 1.0 announcement is modest. "A lot of bugs fixed, a ton of new features, and a complete overhaul of how the jQuery development process is run." There was a Subversion checkout, a bug tracker, a "(Partial) Test Suite," and an update noting that 1.0 arrived "nearly one year after it was first conceived as a post in my weblog." The file header reads "jQuery - New Wave Javascript" and says it is dual licensed under MIT and GPL. The slogan most people associate with the project is not in the file. In 2010 Wikipedia's editors recorded the home page title as "jQuery: The write less, do more, JavaScript library."

Then it moved fast. jQuery 1.1 shipped on the first birthday, January 14, 2007, claiming selectors "10x-20x faster" than 1.0.4 and a simplified API, with a compatibility plugin for people who had already written 1.0 code. GitHub adopted jQuery 1.2.1 in late 2007. And on September 28, 2008, Scott Guthrie announced that "Microsoft will be shipping jQuery with Visual Studio going forward." The jQuery blog added the same day that Nokia would ship it on phones with its web run-time.

Why this one won

There were plenty of JavaScript libraries by 2006, several of them larger and better funded. Here are the forces I think decided it. Each is arguable.

It used a query language people already knew. Anyone who had written a stylesheet could read '#example li'. Prototype's $ took an ID. Willison's function took a selector but handed back a bare array, and you were on your own from there. jQuery took the selector and gave back something you could act on. The people building pages in 2006 were often designers who had learned CSS first, and this was the first JavaScript API written in their language.

It made the set the unit of work. Every method ran on every matched element and returned the set again. That removed the for loop, and it also removed the null check, because a selector that matched nothing gave you an empty set whose methods did nothing. That second property is the one people later turned against it. Hold on to it.

It took the utility belt and hid it. The 1.0 source is a museum of the kind of snippet described in the previous section, sometimes with the author credited in a comment. Here is part of how it decides the document is ready, without waiting for every image as window.onload did:

// If Mozilla is used
if ( jQuery.browser.mozilla || jQuery.browser.opera ) {
  // Use the handy event callback
  document.addEventListener( "DOMContentLoaded", jQuery.ready, false );

// If IE is used, use the excellent hack by Matthias Miller
// http://www.outofhanwell.com/blog/index.php?title=the_window_onload_problem_revisited
} else if ( jQuery.browser.msie ) {

  // Only works if you document.write() it
  document.write("<scr" + "ipt id=__ie_init defer=true " +
    "src=//:><\/script>");

A third branch, for Safari, polls document.readyState on a timer. Three browsers, three unrelated techniques, one of them involving writing a script tag with a nonsense URL into the page. You typed $(document).ready(fn) and never saw any of it. I'd argue this was the real product. The selector engine got the attention, and the hidden branches saved the hours.

It was polite. jQuery kept nearly everything under one global name plus an alias, and it left Object.prototype and Array.prototype alone. It could sit on a page beside another library, which mattered a great deal when the page already had one and you were not allowed to remove it. The documentation for noConflict() still explains the arrangement: "Old references of $ are saved during jQuery initialization; noConflict() simply restores them."

A platform vendor blessed it without taking it over. Guthrie's post is unusually clear about why Microsoft did not build its own. The team looked at adding selectors and animation to ASP.NET AJAX and "quickly realized that the jQuery support for these scenarios is already excellent." So: "We will distribute the jQuery JavaScript library as-is, and will not be forking or changing the source." The ASP.NET MVC download would "add the jQuery library by default to all new projects." For a large population of corporate developers, that sentence moved jQuery from something you had to justify to something that was simply there.

Living with it

Success produced its own set of chores. The first was the dollar sign itself. With two libraries on a page, whoever loaded last owned $. The idiom that solved it is on the same documentation page, and it became the standard way to open a jQuery plugin:

jQuery.noConflict();
(function( $ ) {
  $(function() {
    // More code using $ as alias to jQuery
  });
})(jQuery);

Give the global $ back, then take a private one as a function parameter. It is the same move as the lines at the top of this essay, made by the user instead of the library.

The second chore was upgrades. The 1.1 release, less than five months after 1.0, already needed upgrade guides in three languages and a "jQuery 1.0 Compatibility Plugin." That set a pattern the project kept. Twenty years on, the 4.0 release still ships alongside an upgrade guide and a migration plugin.

The third was the standards process, and here the library authors did something new. In April 2008, with browsers about to ship a native querySelectorAll, Resig wrote to the W3C working group with objections. The main one concerned queries that start from an element. Given this markup:

<div><p id="foo"><span></span></p></div>

asking the foo paragraph for 'div span' returns the span, although there is no div inside the paragraph. The whole document is searched and the results are filtered afterwards. Every library did the opposite. Resig called the native behaviour "completely unacceptable" and "borderline useless to libraries." He had canvassed the other authors, and quoted Andrew Dupont of Prototype: "it violates principle of least surprise and bears no resemblance to the APIs in the wild."

They lost that one. I ran Resig's test case in a current Chromium while writing this, and foo.querySelectorAll('div span') still returns one element. You need to write ':scope div span' to get zero.

What it left behind

The platform copied the homework, slowly. When GitHub removed jQuery in 2018, its engineers listed what had made that possible, and the list reads as jQuery's table of contents translated into standards: "The $(selector) pattern can easily be replaced with querySelectorAll()," class switching with Element.classList, animation in CSS, $.ajax with the Fetch Standard. The dates are worth a look. Selectors API Level 1 became a W3C Recommendation on February 21, 2013, seven and a half years after a student's blog post about fluff. jQuery got .closest() in version 1.3, and Element.closest() is now a standard DOM method with the same name and the same job.

jQuery turned into a polyfill for its own imitation. This is the part I had not put together before reading the source. jQuery 1.3.2, dated February 2009 in its header, already contains this:

if ( !seed && context.nodeType === 9 && !isXML(context) ) {
  try {
    return makeArray( context.querySelectorAll(query), extra );
  } catch(e){}
}

return oldSizzle(query, context, extra, seed);

Try the browser's version, and if it throws, fall back to your own. Notice nodeType === 9. The native path is used only when the query starts from the document, never from an element, which is the case Resig had told the working group was broken. I can't prove that was the motive, and the comments nearby mention a Safari bug as well, but the effect is the same. The library adopted the standard where the standard agreed with it and routed around it everywhere else. We now call this pattern a polyfill or progressive enhancement. In 2009 it was a library quietly making itself less necessary, one try block at a time.

The empty set became the argument against it. GitHub's post gives a three-line example, $('.js-widget').addClass('is-loading').show(), and then asks: "Did the author expect one or more js-widget elements on this page?" If the class name vanishes from the markup, nothing fails. "By default, jQuery silently skips the whole expresion when nothing matched the initial selector; but to us, such behavior was a bug rather than a feature." They also found that chaining "doesn't lend itself well to static analysis, since almost every result of a jQuery method call is of the same type." The feature that made jQuery pleasant for one person on one page was the same feature that made it hard for hundreds of engineers and a type checker. My own reading is that the language later settled on a compromise. Optional chaining, el?.classList.add(), is jQuery's silent no-op made opt-in, one question mark at a time.

The dollar sign outlived the dependency. Open the console in Chrome on a page with no libraries and type $('img'). It works. Chrome's documentation lists $(selector) as "a shortcut for the document.querySelector() function," with a note that if the page uses "a library such as jQuery that uses $, this functionality will be overwritten." The tool yields the name to the library, the way the library once yielded it to Prototype.

It is still most of the web. W3Techs, on November 12, 2026, has jQuery on 63.9% of all websites, and 16.9% of those jQuery sites are still on version 1. The project is not a ruin either. jQuery 4.0.0 came out on January 17, 2026, "the first major version release in almost 10 years," dropping support for Internet Explorer 10 and older while keeping IE 11 for one more round. The retreat has mostly happened among people who write new code. Bootstrap 5 shipped in May 2021 under the heading "No more jQuery!" The site You Might Not Need jQuery is careful about its own scope: "jQuery and its cousins are great, and by all means use them if it makes it easier to develop your application." Its plea is aimed at library authors who add a dependency for three function calls.

One more thing in that 2015 look back deserves attention. Resig wrote that "jQuery would not have existed if it wasn't for Sam Stephenson creating Prototype, Simon Willison creating getElementsBySelector, Valerio Proietti creating moo.fx, and especially Dean Edwards creating so much: event binding, CSS selector libraries, DOM ready techniques and more." Take him at his word and jQuery contained very little that was new. Selectors in JavaScript existed. $ existed. The event fix was a contest entry. What Resig added was the counting: the decision that the right API was the one with the least text between the thing you meant and the thing you had to type. Does that count as invention? I think it does, and I think it is the kind that standards bodies are worst at and individuals with a blog are best at.

The takeaway

The dollar sign replaced two things. On the page, it replaced the utility belt: the pasted addEvent(), the onload hack, the ActiveXObject wrapper, each with its author's name in a comment and its own set of bugs. jQuery gathered them behind one function and one query language that every CSS author already knew, and it was polite enough to coexist with whatever was on the page before it arrived. That combination, more than any single feature, is why it won.

In the longer run it replaced the process by which the web platform got fixed. In 2005 that process was a blog contest. By 2008 it was a library author writing to a W3C list on behalf of his users, and by 2013 the selector function was a W3C Recommendation. jQuery's reward for being right was to become optional. It is hard to think of a better outcome for a library, or a rarer one, and it is still loading on roughly two pages out of three while you decide whether you need it.
